I was wondering what your opinion of this was. Is it a good or bad thing to give players a tonne of options when it comes to settings and gameplay.

Would it be better to offer a very focused designed gameplay experience instead.

Does it depend on the game, or is there a way to offer both at the same time.
Giving the player as many options as possible. A good or bad thing?

I think linearity can really help with a narrative. Not to spoil anything, but the first Bioshock and the Half-Life series do this very well. It's a lot easier to tell one story than to make a bunch of stories. The linearity actually fits the theme and adds a certain "feel" to the gameplay.

On the other hand, I like games with a lot of options, but it's very rare for it to have any serious effect on the story. And I can't seem to actually finish open-world games, because I'm always fucking around. Since I don't spend a lot of time playing video games, I prefer a game with a clear endpoint that I can finish in a couple sessions.

There was a very specific developer in my mind when I was coming up with this question, and that is Arcen games, who provide a tonne of customisation and options in all of their games, and as much as I enjoy that, you are right that their narrative really falls short.

Also I get this very strange feeling that once I'm given all the variables and settings to play around with in a game, it takes some of the magic away, because it's like I'm looking past the shiny exterior into the cogs and gears of the game, and I know how everything works. Takes some of the mystery out of it.

I've never heard of those guys, but I'll have to look into that. I mod the shit out of my games so there's not much magic to begin with for me. But I see your point. I remember with older console games there really wasn't much to change in the game, and games did seem more magical. Maybe it's just my rose-tinted glasses.

And often with RPGs that allow the player leeway in how the story goes, there's one path that stands out as being better written than the others. For example, KOTOR 2 is better with a light-side or neutral male exile than any other combo. Disciple just isn't as good a character as Handmaiden, and playing as a dark side character doesn't really make sense given the villains in the story.

I think it's another example of everything in moderation. I don't mind lots of customization but I almost always just stick to the basics and never completely define a face. I do tend to get turned off when there's too much to do in terms of missions, side quests, and activities and things like that though. I also like games where it's one long straight story like Enchanted Arms.

So I think what I'm trying to say is it's a matter of finding the right balance.

In terms of settings, I'm always for MORE MORE MORE. As for gameplay, it depends on the game.

I mean really, look at TF2. It's a bit ridiculous at times, but I love giving the player as many options in terms of settings as possible. FOV sliders are my best friend. No I actually didn't play with that, my FOV in that game is only 150. But I love being able to play in a way that gives me an edge specific to my style of play.

Looking at something like Mass Effect versus something like Skyrim, I think ME got it right. By comparison ME is on rails, but gives you enough options while still keeping you on a general track to follow and finish the game.

Looking at Crysis against Crysis 2 or 3.... It's not even fair. Crysis basically gave you a destination and you could choose your own route and method to it. The rest are basically rail shooters.

I'd like to see more TPS and FPS in the Mass Effect/Spec Ops The Line range where I get choices whether or not they actually make a difference should and could vary, but giving simple choices in games like this really give the single player elements a new life.

Structured variety. Extended credits from penny arcade did a great bit on how variety is great, but then someone finds a meta and burns the shut out of it for the whole game. They may enjoy it but it gets stale. Giving hem options to overcome some onstacle where the meta does not work is great. For that, you sometimes have to limit the options in game.

It really depends how you set it up. For instance, this works well in a open world RPG, by preparing for the maximum amount of scenarios, you can allow the story to progress no matter what choice the player chooses. However, in a closed world, where the player can only explore a small, controlled area, this may overwhelm the player, and lead them to abandon the game in favor of a better game.

You should always give as many ways as possible for the player to accomplish their goals. The truly amazing thing about Deus Ex was the amount of choice you had in the game, despite it being incredibly linear. It's a big reason while I think Mass Effect is overrated. Sure, you can go down the specializations to develop different ways to kill people, but basically every level is going to be a firefight. There's no sneaking option, there's no trapping option, you just choose your preferred way of shooting them. The "choices" in the dialogue are also pretty weak. Originally, I thought when they were making paragon-renegade dichotomy that it would be a law-chaos axis instead of good-evil. Sadly no. They could have just as well made it entirely (or almost entirely) scripted and give Shepard a stronger character.

Which gets to the crux of the issue. The more choices you give the player, story-wise, the weaker the personality of the main character (MC). You couldn't have Cloud Strife or Solid Snake with a branching story-line. Visual novels are the easiest examples of this. Any time MC has a real personality the player is given very few decision points. Song of Saya, Fate/Stay Night, and the Fruit of the Grisaia all come to mind. At the same time, sometimes you want to feel like you are MC. That gives you a JC Denton-type of character with cool lines but no personality because you are the personality. Same thing with MC in the real Fallout games (don't get me started on FO3. Also discounting the FO Tactics games). And, again, you have that uncomfortable middle ground like MC in KOTOR where you're railroaded really strongly into being the good guy or the bad guy and fuck the rest of it.

No options, no game.

Less options, less game.

More options, more believable world and better immersion.

No reason to not have options.

The balance between the two is not easy to achieve. It depends if the game is intended to be a playful sandbox with a large open world or a smaller less open world. Narrative style also needs to be tailored to suit the choices. Large open world games often fall flat with their story.

Separate missions from the sandbox can make the game feel like it is split in two parts. The goofy sandbox and the serious missions with parameters that must be met. This is very apparent in the GTA series where you can do what the hell you want outside of missions. During the missions you're forced to do certain things in a certain order.

One way is to split the game into levels or separate areas. Each area is open but it either has branching paths or it funnels you to a specific doorway which leads to the next larger area. This is the way Hitman: Absolution, Batman and Metal Gear Solid did it.

Depends, it's better to get a good balance and really depends on the type of game you're making. RPGs, the more options the better. FPSs, they seem too overwhelming when you have too many options, no matter how fun the core gameplay is (COD: AW would be an example for me). Linear games seem to lend to more indepth singular narratives (Halo) which can then be explored further, whereas others just create massive universes with many, many much simpler stores (ESO). The genre I think plays a huge hand in what the right balance is.

Depends on the game, and how they want the story within (if there even is one) to unfold. Take for instance and given Elder Scrolls game. The highlight is not the main story mode. That's not usually how most people learn about the environment and the story. The open exploration and slow discovery of lore and characters is how most people prefer to understand the story. If the main story is the main driving goal of the game, less options is better so the player can focus more on the story, and not get bogged down with other things.

I think it comes down to the type of game, and the price. For example, when it comes to stealth games(purely stealth games, not necessarily action-stealth games though I'm sure to some extent the same applies for them too), the player most likely will want as many options as possible. They will want the choice in how to approach a situation.

However, there are genres that people will find a vast amount of gameplay options to be overwhelming, so you might want to give them less.

Naturally though, when you pay more money, you expect to get more out of it.

I enjoy having lots of options. it makes roleplaying or replaying a game more enjoyable. From my experience, most people when giving a lot of options and choices will use every single one. For me, I will only use what fits the narrative of my roleplaying. Such as only using one gun for fallout as if it has sentimental value to it while having no points in guns.

less options for me mean one play through

As for settings, I hate when video games don't allow me to remap my buttons, or change resolution, or sound volume. In my opinion there should be two options for menus: basic, and advanced, and you should be able to reset to the default with ease.

As for gameplay, it depends on what you're going for. You need to strike a balance. If there's too little to do it's boring. If there's too much to do then it's too complicated. Right now I feel as if games are getting too complicated. They're usually hard to pick up, and play. It's not like the NES.

Borderless windowed mode is really important to me.

A few moments ago, as I took a nightly toke following a day of errands, shopping, job applications, exercise, and healthy eating, I found myself thinking -- "I think marijuana has played a not insignificant role in my ability to feel like a productive member of society." Followed very closely by thinking how much that statement rings true of drug users and medication takers both.

There's got to be a line somewhere, delineating "necessary medication" and "addiction". They are, to some degree, extremely similar. Alcoholics feel they need booze in order to feel like a society member, and we classify that as an addiction. Whereas, for a chronically ill person, their daily drug use is typically seen as medication.

Marijuana, in this sense, walks the really fine line between recreational activity and medicine (What other drug can really say that? Is there any?). While marijuana may not present any withdrawal symptoms, a case could be made for addictive tendencies of the psychological variety -- that is, in the sense that some feel they need the drug in order to function societally. A yet more powerful case can be made for it's medical qualities. So how, on an individual and/or societal level, do we make the distinction between a daily dose for medical reasons, or a daily hit for an addict?

As we approach legalization on an increasingly frequent state-by-state basis, and perhaps quite soon on a federal level in the United States, this blurred line between recreational and medical use will have to be brought into sharper focus. Especially for any of us Elder Ents, who have gone beyond initial use of the substance and must work out how to incorporate it into our mature lives, this line becomes increasingly important. It will be necessary to define in order to pass on a healthy respect for the newest recreational drug to the first generation of humans who never knew it illegally, or else we potentially risk this generation overusing, or abusing. How would we explain the delineation to our children? How do we communicate responsible use? Surely, the responsible use of an anxiety medication for a chronic condition would be daily use. Can we rely on doctors to notice those faking anxiety for a license (and an excuse to use) and those who truly have the disorder?

We have an opportunity to place the line for the next generation in a way that hasn't happened in our human memory. How will you define it?
A fine line between addiction and medication

I agree that the definition is quite indistinct. It's a question I often ask myself, and I haven't yet found an answer.

I don't, however, think that cannabis legalization is going to have far-reaching effects on our definitions of addiction. Yes, we talk of alcoholics and smoking addiction, but caffeine addiction is a joke. Caffeine is almost benefit-free, since your body adjusts to your habitual use, and comes with side effects and withrawal.

Addiction is a very slippery word; it is used in many contexts to mean many things. A psychological addiction (a habit) is considered a health problem when it interferes with normal functioning, yet many people maintain "functional alcoholic" status, or need caffeine every morning. To define addiction in those terms means it becomes more subjective, requiring people to be honest with themselves and have the insight to recognize a harmful addiction despite rationalizations.

If you define addiction in terms of net harm, many things can be daily habits without meeting the definition. If a substance truly improves one's quality of life, then why not? Unfortunately, quality of life is also subjective, and measuring it requires the same introspection and insight.

I don't think that subjectivity will go away, at least not without some revolutionary discoveries about the mind and emotions, and the effects of substances on them.

There's an old saying among writers that there's no such thing as a synonym, because the small differences between similar words are always important. I think we should hesitate to use the word 'addiction' for a moment, and replace it with more carefully chosen words that more accurately describe what we are talking about here.

I use MJ medically, to control physically uncomfortable symptoms of chronic disease. I am also one of those people who uses it psychologically too, because I honestly believe it brings out my better nature, and it makes me more able to think and feel things that are healthy and good.

I think we all agree that the medical use of MJ for physical symptoms is no problem, even if it is routine and required for 'normal' living. It's really no different than taking my morning blood pressure pills.

Taking it for psychological improvement is perhaps more troubling, but I think there is a clear distinction to be made here. How do we distinguish a legitimate, psychological medication from a crutch? A person who is depressed for no good reason and who cannot help themselves despite their best effort might improve significantly on prozac, and that's not a problem, that's a blessing. By the same token, a person who medicates away the symptoms of an otherwise treatable condition has built themselves a guided cage. That's the distinction.

The troublesome issue is not that we might need the drug to feel normal, the troublesome issue is if the drug is an inappropriate response to the problem we are fighting. This is almost exactly analogous to the use of pain meds - sometimes they are appropriate, and sometimes not.

This fine line is not specific to drug use, we face it everywhere in our lives. That pizza I want to eat is a fine form of social recreation and stress relief and simple enjoyment, but if I'm using it to suppress my loneliness and insecurity, then it's crossed the line. Note that I chose this example carefully, because chronic overeating will injure and kill you faster than chronic overuse of weed will. This is not a drug-specific problem, its a general life problem that we face everywhere.

Any good thing might be used routinely, and any good thing might be depended upon, without it becoming a bad thing. It's only a concern if it's used as a substitute for a better treatment, or a better choice.
